newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK govt land auction seen measuring confidence.
newsitem.headline: HK govt land auction seen measuring confidence.

text.p: The government's last land auction for the 1996/97 fiscal year was seen as a confidence poll to be cast by local property developers on the future of Hong Kong's property market, analysts said on Monday.
"The auction will be eye-catching due to the timing and the money involved," said Terry Ip, property analyst at BZW Asia.
The government will auction two plots of land on Tuesday, its last sale in the fiscal year ending March 31.
The sites are located at Ho Man Tin in the Kowloon peninsula and at Siu Sai Wan in Hong Kong island's Chai Wan district.
With just three months before the British colony's reversion to Chinese sovereignty and given the large size of the Chai Wan plot, analsysts said the sale would be closely watched.
"We are talking about the market after 1997, and it's a confidence vote," said property analyst Philip Chan at Yamaichi International.

Property consultants and analysts forecast the huge Chai Wan site, zoned for non-industrial usage, was likely to be sold for anything from HK$6.0 billion to HK$14.8 billion (US$775 million to US$1.91 billion).

The wide range reflected differing opinions over whether developers would aim to put luxury housing into the traditionally industrial area, or whether they would go for mass market housing, analysts said.
The 25,592 square metres site with plot ratio estimated at nine times should attract blue-chip developers, while medium-sized developers were likely to bid in teams, they said.
The smaller 2,627 square metre-site in the luxury residential area of Ho Man Tin was expected to fetch between HK$848 million and HK$1.27 billion, analysts said.
Recent fears that local property prices could turn soft would not affect sentiment at the auction, they added.
"Although the local property market is expected to head for a short-term correction, developers are buying for the future," said Yamaichi's Chan.
Developing the sites into residential units would need two to three year at least, well beyond Hong Kong's handover to China at midnight of June 30.
Analysts said the Chai Wan plot might be developed in phases completed from 2000 to 2002.
Fears of an imminent correction on local housing prices have eroded Hong Kong's blue chip Hang Seng Index down more than 1,000 points from its all-time high of 14,004 set in January.
Property prices gained five to 10 percent during the first quarter year after they soared some 20 to 30 percent last year.
They have already surpassed peaks hit on January 1994, which were followed by a sharp market correction in 1994 and 1995.
"Some of the major developers who missed the chance to stock up their land banks in 1995 at cheap prices would certainly like to buy (now)," said BZW's Ip.
